signals.title: Razgatlioglu to miss remainder of the 2026 season
signals.summary: The Prima Pramac rider will undergo surgery and be replaced by test rider Augusto Fernandez Toprak Razgatlioglu travelled to Milan on Monday, October 19, for further medical examinations following the shoulder injury he sustained in a highside crash during the Indonesian Grand Prix at Mandalika. Unfortunately, the latest assessments confirmed that the damage requires surgical treatment to ensure the best possible recovery. In agreement with Toprak, surgery has been scheduled for Monday, October 26, in Milan. Following the procedure, the Turkish rider will focus on his rehabilitation, ruling him out of the Australian Grand Prix at Phillip Island and the remaining rounds of the 2026 MotoGP World Championship. Yamaha test rider Augusto Fernandez is planned to step in for Razgatlioglu for the upcoming races. Yamaha and Prima Pramac Yamaha MotoGP wish Toprak a successful operation and a smooth recovery, and will support him throughout the rehabilitation process and thank Augusto Fernandez for stepping in to help. Gino Borsoi - Team Director, Prima Pramac Yamaha MotoGP: "We are very sorry for Toprak, as we know how much he wanted to race at Phillip Island and continue his journey with the YZR-M1. He has been working hard to adapt to MotoGP, and it is disappointing that this injury will prevent him from continuing that process over the coming races. However, his health must come first, and we will support him throughout his recovery and look forward to seeing him back on the bike when he is ready. At the same time, we welcome Augusto Fernandez, who will step in for Toprak at Phillip Island and until Toprak isn't ready to come back. As Yamaha‘s test rider, he knows the bike well, and we are pleased to have him joining the team for these events. We will work together to make the most of this opportunity while wishing Toprak a successful operation and a smooth recovery" Toprak Razgatlioglu - Prima Pramac Yamaha MotoGP rider: "I‘m extremely disappointed to miss the Australian Grand Prix. Phillip Island is one of my favourite circuits and a place where I‘ve enjoyed some very special moments during my Superbike career. I was excited about the opportunity to race here on the MotoGP bike, which makes this situation even harder to accept. After further medical assessments following the crash in Mandalika, it became clear that my shoulder injury is worse than we first believed. As a result, I will undergo surgery in the coming days to give myself the best chance of making a full recovery and returning at 100%. This wasn‘t an easy decision, but after consulting with the doctors and the people closest to me, we are convinced it is the right step for my future. I would also like to wish Jack all the best for his home Grand Prix. Racing in front of your home crowd is always special, and with this being the final MotoGP event at Phillip Island, I hope he can enjoy a fantastic weekend and achieve a great result. I‘ll be cheering for him and the entire team from afar". Catch all the action from just €29.99 with MotoGP™VideoPass

signals.title: Phillip Island classics: the best of the Australian GP
signals.summary: Sit back and witness five incredible battles we’ve seen at the magical Phillip Island over the years – proving anything can happen Down Under The home of surprises, the home of final lap scraps, the home of drama – MotoGP™ has landed at Phillip Island. Excitement is building, and if last year was anything to go by, we’ve got an unmissable weekend on our hands. There have been so many iconic moments over the years, from shock penalties to final corner deciders, and now you can relive just some of those moments for FREE! Valentino Rossi started the 2003 Australian GP from pole in what would be a memorable day for more than one reason. Marco Melandri took an early lead before getting tangled with Troy Bayliss . Rossi found himself at the front before the GP was turned on its head as the #46 received a 10-second penalty for overtaking under yellow flags. He put the hammer down, beginning one of the most impressive performances we’ve ever seen. Rossi stretched the margin to 15.212s at the flag, making his official winning margin 5.212s over Loris Capirossi and Nicky Hayden . Valentino Rossi is the pre-race favourite heading into this one at the iconic Phillip Island Our trip to Phillip Island in 2004 brought another instalment of Valentino Rossi vs Sete Gibernau . It was drama from lights out, where, after a brave start, Gibernau and Rossi stormed into the distance. The pair locked horns until the final lap, with everything being decided on the run to the flag. Rossi snatched victory from Gibernau, winning by just 0.097s. This was enough for Rossi to become the 2004 MotoGP World Champion, completing the first chapter of what would become a remarkable switch to Yamaha. Relive the classic Australian Grand Prix at the Phillip Island Circuit in 2004. Drama. The only word which can be used to describe the 2013 Australian GP. With a mandatory bike swap in place for safety reasons, Jorge Lorenzo took the lead on the opening laps after launching from pole. The key moment arrived when the field began to pit, with Marc Marquez remaining out until the end of Lap 11. This was outside the window, with the #93 receiving a black flag, resulting in disqualification. Lorenzo stormed to victory, beating Dani Pedrosa and Valentino Rossi, even if the headlines were made by the #93. Relive the premier class race at the 2013 Tissot Australian Grand Prix at Phillip Island Overtakes, high-speed drama and unbelievable moves, the 2015 Australian GP had it all, with a whole host of manufacturers fighting for glory. Marc Marquez started the GP from pole, with Andrea Iannone stealing the advantage in the opening stages on board the Ducati. Both Jorge Lorenzo and Marquez took turns at the front, with Valentino Rossi also in the mix. Lorenzo led onto the final lap from Marquez, with the #93 setting up a spectacular move at Lukey Heights, stealing victory as Lorenzo took second and Iannone third. Relive the premier class race at the 2015 Pramac Australian Grand Prix at Phillip Island Our visit to Phillip Island came at the perfect time in 2022, with tension rising as just a handful of points separated Francesco Bagnaia and Fabio Quartararo in the World Championship. Jorge Martin led the opening laps before Quartararo hit the deck on Lap 11. Meanwhile, Alex Rins , Bagnaia and Marc Marquez battled for glory in true Australian GP fashion. Rins held firm, charging to victory over Marquez and Bagnaia – pure drama. It's main event time at Phillip Island as the lights go out in Round 18 of the MotoGP™ World Championship Like what you’ve seen? Don’t worry, we’ve got you covered as we head Down Under with just two points separating Martin and Marc Marquez. See you there! Catch all the action from just €29.99 with MotoGP™VideoPass

signals.title: MotoGP set for high-speed showcase at the Formula 1 United States Grand Prix 2026
signals.summary: Two wheels meet four at one of the world’s greatest racetracks in Austin, Texas MotoGP will bring the world's fastest motorcycles to the FORMULA 1 MSC CRUISES UNITED STATES GRAND PRIX 2026 at Circuit of The Americas (COTA), with four premier-class machines set to take to the track for a high-speed demonstration on Saturday. Capable of speeds exceeding 225mph and lean angles of more than 60 degrees, MotoGP bikes represent the pinnacle of two-wheel racing. In a landmark moment for global motorsport, the demonstration and wider fan activations will see the inclusion of MotoGP during a Formula 1 Grand Prix weekend for the first time, in front of a crowd of more than 400,000 fans expected across the event. MotoGP Hall of Fame inductee Dani Pedrosa (KTM), 2027 MotoGP rider and current WorldSBK World Champion Nicolo Bulega (Ducati), and MotoGP test riders Andrea Dovizioso (Yamaha) and Lorenzo Savadori (SuperFile Trackhouse MotoGP Team) will take to the iconic Austin circuit, giving Formula 1 fans a rare opportunity to experience the speed and sound of MotoGP up close, with bikes capable of producing more than 130 decibels of noise. The showcase will take place on Saturday, 24 October, from 11:40am to 12:00pm CDT, with riders completing high-speed laps around COTA ahead of Free Practice 3. With the MotoGP World Championship competing in Australia on the same weekend, the showcase provides a unique opportunity to bring MotoGP directly to one of the biggest sporting events in the United States and one of the most attended motorsport weekends in the world. In addition to the on-track action, MotoGP will host a dedicated fan activation in the circuit Fan Zone throughout the weekend, featuring the four motorcycles on display and opportunities for fans to get closer to the sport. MotoGP teams and riders will be onsite from Thursday through Sunday as the championship continues to build momentum towards its 2027 Grand Prix of the United States, which returns to COTA from April 23-25, 2027. Dani Pedrosa, who won three Grand Prix World Championships across the 125cc and 250cc classes, said: "It's always special to ride a MotoGP bike at COTA, one of the most iconic circuits in the world. "The United States Grand Prix is a truly unique and special event on the F1 calendar, attracting an incredible crowd and providing a great opportunity to give fans a taste of what makes MotoGP so exciting. The speed, the sound and the performance of these bikes is something you have to experience in person, and I'm looking forward to sharing that with everyone in Austin." Nicolo Bulega, current WorldSBK World Champion with Ducati, who will make the switch to compete in MotoGP next season as part of Pertamina Enduro VR46 Racing Team, added: “This is a fantastic opportunity to put MotoGP in front of one of the biggest crowds in world motorsport. The atmosphere at COTA is always incredible, and to ride a MotoGP bike in front of so many fans will be a special experience. "MotoGP bikes are unlike anything else, and hopefully the laps will show just how spectacular our sport is. We're looking forward to putting on a great show and giving fans a glimpse of what they can expect when I return with MotoGP to Austin in 2027."

signals.title: MotoGP 2027 rider line-up: the grid is set!
signals.summary: Signed and sealed, the 2027 grid is confirmed! Find out who’s moving where ahead of MotoGP’s new era As 2026 enters its closing stages, we’ve got concrete news from all 11 teams with regard to 2027. We’ve put all the news, signings and seats in one place so you can familiarise yourself with who is in what colours for next year. If you’ve missed any announcements, don’t worry, we’ve got you covered below! The reigning World Champions will retain their very own reigning World Champion in Marc Marquez until at least 2028 . The Spaniard will have a new teammate in the form of Pedro Acosta, who moves from KTM machinery . ‘The Shark’ will also be in Ducati red until at least 2028 . The current Championship leaders confirmed Marco Bezzecchi on a multi-year deal ahead of the Sepang Test at the start of 2026, but his teammate was confirmed at the Dutch GP: Francesco Bagnaia . The double World Champion has a four-year deal with the Noale brand. Fabio Quartararo and Alex Rins have been officially announced as not part of the project from 2027 onwards. In their place, 2024 World Champion Jorge Martin and Japanese sensation – and now MotoGP winner – Ai Ogura. Both have contracts until the end of 2028 . Nadia Padovani’s team have confirmed a fully changed line-up for 2027, mixing MotoGP championship-winning pedigree with youth as Joan Mir and upcoming rookie Daniel Holgado get set to jump on Ducati machinery. Following Pedro Acosta’s departure, Red Bull KTM Factory Racing have announced an all-new lineup for 2027 as Alex Marquez and Fabio Di Giannantonio prepare to make the switch to the Austrian manufacturer for the upcoming season. HRC have their plans sorted for next season, with an all-new rider line-up to look forward to. Fabio Quartararo will join the squad from 2027 , with Diogo Moreira alongside as the Brazilian makes the step from LCR . There will be a shake-up on the management side too, as Alberto Puig leaves his role as team manager and becomes an advisor, being replaced by Mikihiko Kawase. Both sides of Lucio Cecchinello’s box are confirmed, with Johann Zarco penned in for 2027 after signing his deal during the 2025 season. Alongside the experienced Frenchman is MotoGP rookie David Alonso , who makes the step up from Moto2 after signing a multi-year deal with HRC. It’s exciting times over at the SuperFile Trackhouse MotoGP Team, with the American squad announcing that they will continue to work with Raul Fernandez until the end of 2028 . His teammate? Enea Bastianini. The Beast enters the SuperHouse in 2027, ensuring Trackhouse have experienced, race-winning pedigree on both sides of the box going into next year. Everything is confirmed over at Red Bull KTM Tech3, with Luca Marini joining Guenther Steiner’s team from 2027 . His teammate? None other than Moto2 star Senna Agius, creating the perfect mix between experience and a fresh perspective. We’ve also had confirmation that Tech3 will race with KTM machinery from 2027 and beyond following a multi-year agreement. Signed and sealed at the VR46 Racing Team. Fermin Aldeguer has been confirmed at the Italian squad , remaining on board a Ducati for 2027 and 2028 as the #54 moves from Gresini. He’ll be joined by WorldSBK’s Championship leader Nicolo Bulega , who makes the jump from Superbike to the Grand Prix paddock – completing a very bright fluo yellow line-up! Paolo Campinoti’s team is looking strong for 2027. Rookie Toprak Razgatlioglu heads into his second season with the team and took part in the tyre test on Monday after the Czech GP with the new 850cc prototype. The recently announced second seat will be taken by Moto2™ graduate Izan Guevara, who makes his move to the premier class after four seasons in Moto2. There we have it. The final piece of the puzzle is in place, and the countdown has already begun for MotoGP's new era. First, one final push in 2026 before we welcome the class of 2027. Don’t miss out! signals.title: Honda HRC Castrol confirm Moreira alongside Quartararo for 2027
signals.summary: The #11 will race in the factory squad alongside the 2021 World Champion It’s official: Honda Racing Corporation have announced that Diogo Moreira will join the Honda HRC Castrol factory team for 2027! As part of a multi-year agreement, he’ll line up alongside Fabio Quartararo as a new era begins. A post shared by Commonwealth Games 2022 (@gamescommonwealth) The 22-year-old Brazilian steps up from LCR Honda, where he has spent his rookie premier-class season after signing an HRC contract off the back of his impressive Moto2 World Championship campaign. With five wins, 13 podiums and nine pole positions across the lightweight and middleweight classes, Moreira’s trajectory from entering the World Championship in 2022 to MotoGP in 2026 has been meteoric. Crowned Moto2 World Champion in 2025 in just his fourth season racing on the world stage, a breakthrough first Moto2 victory at Assen saw him fight back through the standings to take the title. The blend of raw speed, race craft and composure under pressure convinced HRC he was ready for the premier class and a clear star of the future. His first year in MotoGP has confirmed that judgement. Moreira approached the season with a clear plan and built his confidence and understanding of the Honda RC213V step by step until a breakout weekend at the Catalan GP where he achieved his first top ten finish. Since then, he has consistently battled for top Honda honours in the majority of races. A debut Sprint podium at HRC’s home race in Motegi proved he was ready for the factory team. The #11 will join Quartararo in the Honda HRC Castrol team on a multi-year contract as MotoGP transitions to a new set of technical regulations. A combination of proven success and youthful promise, the 2027 Honda HRC Castrol line up heads into the new season with the objective of returning Honda HRC back to the top of the MotoGP World Championship standings. Moreira will not be the first Brazilian to ride for the factory Honda squad in the premier class, Alex Barros earning four podiums during the 2004 MotoGP season with the Honda RC211V. Diogo Moreira: “It is a fantastic feeling to arrive to the factory Honda HRC team in MotoGP, it is something that every rider dreams of when they are young. I want to say thank you to everyone in Honda HRC for putting their faith in me and making the next step in this project. So far in 2026 we have done a great job to adapt to the bike and the sensations for the future are already very positive from what we have seen. Of course, I must also say thank you to everyone in LCR who have helped me in my adaptation to MotoGP – the whole team has been crucial in this development. I am looking forward to next year and to helping Honda HRC return to where they must be.” Yuzura Ishikawa, General Manager, Motorcycle Racing Division, HRC: “Moreira has always been able to adapt to new bikes quickly, everything from motocross to Moto3, Moto2 and now MotoGP. This is the sign of a talented rider and as HRC, we aim to keep supporting Diogo in the next step of his career and in the next step of our plan to return to fighting for the World Championship. We have a highly competitive rider line-up next season across Honda HRC Castrol and the LCR Team and I am sure that all of these riders will push each other not only to raise their level on track, but also to help HRC’s engineers create the best bike possible in this new era of racing.” Catch all the action from just €29.99 with MotoGP™VideoPass

signals.title: Lecuona steps in for Aldeguer in Australia
signals.summary: The #54 will be sidelined to recover, with the WorldSBK race winner stepping in at Gresini once again Fermin Aldeguer will be sidelined from the Australian GP following his recent hand injury. The #54 returned to Spain after his crash on Sunday in Indonesia and underwent surgery, and he’s now full steam ahead on recovery in time for the Malaysian GP at Sepang. “I had bad luck this year, now with my hand,” Aldeguer recently told the WorldSBK team at Jerez, underlining his first target back. “It’s less than one week after the injury so we have to stay calm and see if I can be back in Malaysia. It’s our first goal. We will see.” In the meantime, Iker Lecuona will step in for Aldeguer this weekend for the Red Bull Australian GP. It’s the third time the SBK Ducati rider returns to the BK8 Gresini Racing MotoGP team this season, after subbing for Alex Marquez at Balaton and Aldeguer at Silverstone. signals.title: HOT HEADLINES: the final Phillip Island battle beckons for tight 2026 title fight
signals.summary: A last chapter of history will be written as Phillip Island brings the end of the title showdown ever closer Phillip Island first showed us what it was all about in 1989 and has been the host of the Australian GP since 1997. Countless memories, showdowns and runs to the line have been witnessed in that time. Before we bid farewell to ‘The Island’ and write a new chapter in Adelaide from 2027, we could well be in for one of the most important Grands Prix of the season so far. Two points is the difference between two rivals who battled hard here two years ago, and the stakes couldn’t be higher as the title race gets set for five GPs in six weeks where by the end of it all, one champion will be crowned. Just two points separate Martin and Marquez as the title fight shifts into overdrive. At Phillip Island, the next plot twist is never far away You’d have been a brave pundit to predict that Marc Marquez (Ducati Lenovo Team) would leave Mandalika with the exact same two-point deficit as when he entered but that’s what the reigning Champion did. An Aprilia 1-2-3-4 on Sunday, with Jorge Martin (Aprilia Racing) in third kept the Martinator ahead and whilst Aprilia were strong in Australia last year, it’ll be new territory on the RS-GP for the #89. What we can hope for is a repeat of their epic, Grand Prix-of-the-season battle from 2024, that time going the way of the #93. As for 2026, Martin remains with just one victory but has been on the Grand Prix podium in the last three whilst Marquez only has six Sunday podiums – all of them victories. It wasn’t long ago that Bezzecchi ’s title hopes seemed to be fading but he, like Martin, has been on the podium in the last three GPs and finally got back to Grand Prix winning ways at Mandalika. Five of the last six GPs on the rostrums and Phillip Island’s Sprint winner from 2025, the #72 is 46 points back from Martin but still very much determined in his bid for the title. He’s 50 clear of Ai Ogura (SuperFile Trackhouse MotoGP Team), making it a realistic three-horse title fight with five rounds remaining. This was the part of the season last year where Bezzecchi seemed to have an extra gear and hit the form he carried into the early part of 2026 - can he do it again one year on? We look back at some of their very best battles while we wait for some more in the final part of the season as the title fight between the two Spaniards heats up! Ogura is fourth by a single point over Austrian GP winner Pedro Acosta (Red Bull KTM Factory Racing), with the Spaniard not having the happiest of times in Japan or Indonesia. The battle for fourth is a four-way fight with Fabio Di Giannantonio (Pertamina Enduro VR46 Racing Team) in hot pursuit whilst Raul Fernandez ’s (SuperFile Trackhouse MotoGP Team) P2 at Mandalika reignites his charge. The #25 won in MotoGP for the first time at Phillip Island last year and it was Diggia who clinched P2 just behind, so 2026 could be interesting. Alex Marquez (BK8 Gresini MotoGP Team), teammate Fermin Aldeguer and double World Champion Francesco Bagnaia (Ducati Lenovo Team) complete the top ten in the standings, but Aldeguer is once again on the sidelines after his hand injury picked up in Lombok, replaced by Iker Lecuona as he was earlier in the year. Enea Bastianini (Red Bull KTM Tech3) is just two points behind Aldeguer in the top ten battle overall and fellow countryman Luca Marini (Honda HRC Castrol) is just a further 14 behind, hoping he can keep his streak of points in every GP in 2026 going Down Under. Brad Binder (Red Bull KTM Factory Racing) is just four points off Marini too, and has been a top eight finisher in the last three Australian Grands Prix, whilst top Yamaha Fabio Quartararo (Monster Energy Yamaha MotoGP) has enjoyed points in the last two Grands Prix and Sprints. Bezzecchi returns to winning ways at Mandalika as Aprilia delivers a landmark Sunday, locking out the top four for the first time in MotoGP Top rookie in 2026 Diogo Moreira (Pro Honda LCR) is tied on points with Quartararo and just 15 ahead of Franco Morbidelli (Pertamina Enduro VR46 Racing Team), who in-turn is just eight ahead of 2023 Australian GP winner Johann Zarco (Castrol Honda LCR). All home eyes will be on Jack Miller (Prima Pramac Yamaha MotoGP), however. He’ll aim to bow out of MotoGP with one final strong showing at his home Grand Prix, where he was mighty close to the Sprint podium in 2025. Teammate Toprak Razgatlioglu won’t be in action after requiring surgery following his crash at the Indonesian GP. Razgatlioglu will miss the remainder of the season, with Yamaha test rider Augusto Fernandez stepping in at Prima Pramac Yamaha MotoGP. Meanwhile, Alex Rins (Monster Energy Yamaha MotoGP) remains one of five Australian GP winners lining up on the grid, the other being Maverick Viñales (Red Bull KTM Tech3), who is also looking for more as he rebuilds from a long layoff. Joan Mir ’s (Honda HRC Castrol) attendance remains to be confirmed by Honda as he struggles with illness, so stay tuned for an update there. Two points at the top, another key contender with an impressive form book and five GPs in six weeks await. There's plenty more to come in 2026 so get ready for another awesome, and final, show from the Island. Catch all the action from just €29.99 with MotoGP™VideoPass

signals.title: Curtain closer: MotoJunior celebrates triple title showdown at Misano
signals.summary: Misano served up five stunning races on the Adriatic Coast, crowning three new Champions and closing out the 2026 season! It was a day of drama, final-lap thrillers and title-winning celebrations as Misano hosted the 2026 season finale. Carlos Cano, Alvaro Lucas and Lorenzo Fellon entered the spotlight, celebrating their crowning moments as Milan Pawelec ended his Moto2 ECh season in style, adding to his astonishing win tally. After an incredible day of racing, catch up with everything from Round 7! Fernando Bujosa (AC Racing Team) completed a perfect weekend at Misano with two victories, extending his winning streak to three races following his maiden triumph at Aragon. The Spaniard dominated Race 1, finishing 1.369s clear of Kiattisak Singhapong (Honda Asia-Dream Racing Junior Team), who earned second, whilst Yaroslav Karpushin (CFMOTO Aspar Junior Team) was third. Carlos Cano (CFMOTO Aspar Junior Team) was crowned the 2026 Moto3 Junior World Champion following a P6 finish in Race 1. Race 2 proved a much closer affair, with Bujosa edging out Kiandra Ramadhipa (Honda Asia-Dream Racing Junior Team) by just 0.006s following a spectacular three-way drag to the line. Karpushin crossed the line just 0.019s further back to round out the podium. Milan Pawelec (AGR Team) celebrated the perfect end to 2026, sprinting to his eighth victory of the season. The #44 had plenty of support at Misano, ending the year with a 45-point advantage over nearest rival Unai Orradre (Momoven Racing). Francesco Mongiardo (MMR) returned to the podium, ending his home weekend in second. Meanwhile, Facundo Llambias (Team Estrella Galicia 0,0) completed the top three, earning his first podium since Magny-Cours last season. Alessandro Morosi (EAGLE-1) took fourth, clinching third in the Moto2 European Championship in the process. Lorenzo Pritelli (Team Echovit Pasini Racing) celebrated the dream Sunday at Misano, storming to the top spot at his home round. Pritelli took victory by an impressive 7.021s margin in the season finale. Ethan Sparks (British Talent Team – GRYD) chased behind, crossing the line in second and clinching his first podium in the Momoven Moto4 European Cup. Sparks charged from P15 on the grid and ended the season with added silverware. Victor Cubeles (Team Impala Honda) rounded out the podium, ending the season with a fourth rostrum finish. However, the headlines surrounded Alvaro Lucas (CFMOTO Aspar Junior Team), who was crowned the 2026 Momoven Moto4 European Cup Champion after a P7 finish on Sunday afternoon. Jacobo Hinojosa (Futurotel Face Racing) brought the Stock European Championship season to a close with victory in the sole race at Misano, while Lorenzo Fellon (SF Racing) did enough to secure the 2026 title with a fifth-place finish, capping off a memorable campaign for the Frenchman. Championship runner-up Yeray Ruiz (Team Honda Laglisse) kept the pressure on until the very end, taking second place in the race but ultimately falling just nine points short of the title after a closely contested Championship battle. Marcos Ludeña (IUM Motorsports) rounded out the podium with a breakthrough performance, fighting his way through from a career-best sixth on the grid to claim his maiden Stock European Championship podium in the final race of the season. And that’s it! The 2026 FIM MotoJunior World Championship comes to a thrilling conclusion, with anticipation already building towards 2027. See you soon! signals.title: 2027 FIM MotoJunior World Championship calendar released
signals.summary: The MotoJunior World Championship is gearing up for more in 2027, with a new destination on the horizon The 2027 FIM MotoJunior World Championship calendar is here! Racing across Portugal, Spain, Czechia, Italy and France, 2027 promises excitement from the very start. With seven rounds and a brand-new destination on the calendar, the next generation will have plenty of opportunities to make their mark on the Road to MotoGP™. The 2027 season starts at the beginning of May, with the Circuito do Estoril set to host the opening round. From there, it’s a busy June as the MotoJunior paddock heads to the Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya before a historic first visit to Brno a few weeks later. MotoJunior will not visit the classic Circuito de Jerez-Angel Nieto in 2027 due to works to be undertaken on its facilities, but the Championship returns for more in September, with MotorLand Aragon holding the penultimate round of the season. The paddock then heads to the Circuit Ricardo Tormo for the grand finale in Valencia. Check out the 2027 calendar in detail as another exhilarating season on the Road to MotoGP™ awaits! signals.title: “When I walked down from Parc Ferme to my box, even the sky was crying”
signals.summary: Catch up on the best debriefs from an emotional Sunday at Jerez was riders reflected on the final race day of 2026 The 2026 MOTUL FIM Superbike World Championship was one for the history books. It came to an end at the Circuito de Jerez - Angel Nieto, Andalucia and tears started to flow after the race, almost as much as the rain came down. For some, it was their last race in WorldSBK; for others, their future still hasn’t been confirmed. Read the best debriefs from the Pirelli Spanish Round below. Jerez marked the end of the road for Danilo Petrucci in WorldSBK, who said: “I’m really happy to get to the end of this journey. It’s been incredible. I didn’t expect all of this. When you’re a child, you want to become a World Champion, but it’s not easy. I’m so happy with what I’ve achieved and I can be proud. Unfortunately, this year, the outcome wasn’t good, but everyone gave their best. For a guy coming from the Italian countryside, it’s something that I can be proud to have won in MotoGP, then switch to Dakar and win a stage, then go back to track racing and winning a WorldSBK race, it’s something that fulfilled my dreams. The first podium at Donington, the first win at Cremona, fighting for the top guys… there are many highlights. I’m satisfied and proud to be a factory rider with BMW. There’s a life after racing and I want to enjoy it. Since I joined BMW, everything that could go wrong has gone wrong. I signed with BMW the day Iannone made a big mistake in Hungary in Race 1. We started to fight for third in the Championship, then I got injured. In my right hand now, I have three plates and 20 screws. I’ve had really bad accidents in the last three years, and operations and physiotherapy. I fought with my body. No winter testing, and when we started to get better, I got injured. I missed three rounds and two tests. Maybe I’m most proud this afternoon, when I walked down from Parc Ferme to my box, even the sky was crying! It took me 15 minutes because I had to stop at every garage, because everyone was trying to hug me. When I’m asked about my biggest victory, it’s not Mugello or Le Mans or Cremona or Dakar. My biggest victory is to have told a story. If you’re a singer, you always produce music, but it’s another thing when you’re singing a song and you see everyone start to be happy just looking at you, doing what you love the most. It’s something irreplaceable. When you wave and full grandstands go crazy, it’s something you can’t buy.” More records fell Nicolo Bulega’s way after Jerez, and he said: “The Championship was the most important thing. I’ve made a lot of records and today I equalled Bayliss. It’s very special. I can’t choose one moment, everything was special. Everything was perfect. When the rain started, I thought, ‘No, please, I don’t want my last laps in WorldSBK to have a strange end of the race’. When you’re first in those conditions, you don’t know how you can go fast. I realise I’ve finished here, but not 100%. I will stay with my team for a lot of days until the end of the season; we have a lot of things to do together. Maybe I’ll realise in December after the last dinner together. I really liked this livery; I really like when we do something special. Matching Troy is incredible. What can I say? I’ve just finished my third year in WorldSBK and I’m the fifth best of all time. I always had a fantastic bike and team. It was very special to win all these races with Ducati. It was emotional. On the grid, we were all crying. The first two or three laps weren’t easy for me. Danilo is a fantastic guy. I don’t know if he’s finished his career in WorldSBK but, if he has, I’m sorry for him. I just wanted to say hello to him because maybe it was the last race together.” Speaking in Parc Ferme after Race 2 , revealed how emotional he was after crossing the line: “I’m really happy. I want to say thanks to my team after another hat-trick in my last round in WorldSBK. I cried the whole lap after the chequered flag.” A P4 finish for Bautista in Race 2, whose future is still up in the air. He said: “I missed the podium just for a little bit because when it started to rain, it wasn’t all over the track. I didn’t have any reference. Sam behind me had my reference. I slowed down a little bit in some areas, and my tyres cooled down and never recovered. In that moment, I thought it was okay, but it was worse to crash. We were strong. What happened in the last laps with the rain isn’t a usual situation, and this time I had some problems. After a difficult year with a lot of problems, not getting good confidence with the bike and a mid-season injury, it was one of the hardest seasons for me. Inside me, I was confident I was competitive. It was just for me to say that I’m able to go fast. I was quite calm during the race. I wasn’t thinking about it was being last race of the season, with Barni or whether it was my last race. I tried to be focused as if it were a normal race and use the confidence I’d built up over the last two rounds. When I arrived at the box and saw my family and friends, I was a bit emotional. It was like a goodbye, but I don’t feel like I want to say goodbye now. I have to wait a few days to see whether I have something or not. At the moment, there’s nothing clear. I don’t know if I will race and I don’t know if I’ll say goodbye. WorldSBK gave me the chance to show my potential. Honestly, I didn’t want to come, but I wanted to keep racing. I felt my potential was good enough to keep winning. I came here and discovered a different Championship and loved it.” A strong weekend at Jerez for Alex Lowes (bimota by Kawasaki Racing Team), but not enough to beat his brother in the Championship standings. He said: “The livery was nice. It was nice to have a bit of heritage. It’s always scary to change just for the last race, but I thought it looked nice. It didn’t make the bike go any faster, unfortunately, which would’ve been nice! I’m happy for Sam. He had a bad weekend at Estori

signals.title: “I’ve struggled a bit with my consistency… I’ll improve that for 2027” – Sam Lowes ends 2026 on a high note at Jerez
signals.summary: It’s been an up-and-down season for the #14, but he found his mark in the final round British rider Sam Lowes (ELF Marc VDS Racing Team) sent off his 2026 season on a high note, bagging his first podium triple since Aragon, and even snagging a Race 1 silver medal, only the fourth rider to do so in a season where top two finishes have been almost exclusively controlled by factory Ducati bikes. His Pirelli Spanish Round results completed a comeback for fourth place in the Riders’ Championship, a feather in the #14’s cap as he claims bragging rights over his brother Alex Lowes (bimota by Kawasaki Racing Team), who was sent back to a Championship P5 finish at the Circuito de Jerez - Angel Nieto, Andalucia to close the 2026 campaign. It’s been an emotional season for the #14, including the tragic passing of Team Owner and founder Marc van der Straten . Arriving to southern Spain on the heels of a tough round at Estoril in which the #14 took only six Championship points – his worst points haul in a round since Misano back in June – the #14 set the tone early with P2 in the Tissot Superpole session. He outpaced Iker Lecuona (Aruba.it Racing - Ducati) by a tenth to start ahead of him in Race 1 for the first time since Round 9 at Magny-Cours. He put that improved grid start to good use, holding off the #7 through the early laps before settling into a rhythm; by Lap 8, more than two seconds separated them, leading to a second-place finish. A colder, overcast sky greeted the field on track as they set off in their Tissot Superpole Race on Sunday. An overnight step by the factory Ducati #7 saw him see the Brit down to P3 at the Turn 6 overtaking hotspot on the opening lap. As Nicolo Bulega (Aruba.it Racing - Ducati) led the pack ahead of them, Lecuona and Lowes sailed clear of the rest of the pack for the #14 to finish just shy of four seconds behind the Spanish rider, but nearly four seconds clear of Yari Montella (Barni Spark Racing Team) in P4. Race 2 brought out all the stops, while the British rider looked to complete his hat trick. Alvaro Bautista (Barni Spark Racing Team) was determined to close out what has been an uphill 2026 campaign with silverware as his 2027 ride remains unclear . At lights out, the Spaniard enjoyed perhaps his best start of the season, surging from P6 into third. Lowes, however, fell back to fifth into the opening corner as his bike popped a wheelie off the line, costing him vital acceleration into Turn 1. By Turn 6 of the opening laps, he had taken P4 and set his sights on the Spaniard for the bronze-medal position. By Lap 13, he trailed the #19 by as much as 2.6 seconds. Lowes came into his own in the final laps of the session, however. The grey clouds overhead began to produce spots of rain on track by Lap 16, and the Brit clocked a hellacious final five laps. He made up half a second on Lap 16, four tenths on Lap 17, and nearly a second on Lap 18 to force a final-lap battle to the line. He overcame the two-time World Champion at Turn 5 of the final lap to close the season on the podium as the clouds finally let loose a torrential downpour after the flag. On his Sunday fight with Bautista for the final podium of the year, Sam Lowes said: “I’m really happy with the Tissot Superpole Race. I got a bad start in Race 2, I didn’t have quite as good of a feeling, but the pace was strong, Alvaro rode really well. I just kept pushing to the end after trying to save the front tyre over the middle laps. I got a tad lucky with the conditions, but they’re the same for everybody and I’m happy to finish the season like that. I made a couple of mistakes over the middle of the race. From there, I tried to relax and save the tyre. Then, he made a few mistakes, and the rain was coming, so it’s easier to be the guy behind. The last laps felt good. I changed some of the mapping towards the end and came forward a bit. I saw an opening in Turn 5 and made a good move. I feel sorry for Alvaro; he’s done a great job, but in the end, it’s racing, and we’re all trying to finish on the podium. The rain made it hard in the first sector. It got a bit nerve-wracking, as we would push hard in the other sectors but then need to be careful there. We got really, really lucky; we could go at a normal speed, but 3-4 minutes later it became a torrential downpour.” With his podium triple to close the book on 2026, Sam Lowes improved his spot in the standings above his Bimota-powered brother Alex Lowes. He said he would have liked to fight with Yari Montella (Barni Spark Racing Team) for the third spot in the standings, but off-track issues, including the passing of their beloved team boss, and a lack of consistency in the second half of the campaign kept him from doing so. Looking back on his season, Sam Lowes said: “I made many mistakes this season. Of course, it’s also been quite difficult off-track. Over the second half of the season since losing Marc, I’ve struggled a bit with my consistency. Apart from Estoril, I’ve been fast enough at every track. At Estoril, I was slow, but at the rest I was close. I’ll need to work on that for next season. I should have been fighting with Montella for third, but I made too many mistakes, I’ll improve that for 2027.” Watch back through all of the best moments of his season with the WorldSBK VideoPass!

signals.title: Arenas: “Standing on the podium in front of a home crowd is very nice”
signals.summary: The 2026 Champion claimed victory in Race 1 at Jerez after a hard-fought battle with Can Oncu Albert Arenas claimed victory in Race 1 of the FIM Supersport World Championship at the Circuito de Jerez - Angel Nieto, Andalucia after a hard-fought battle. He had to overcome Can Oncu in the first half of the race before a hard-charging and in-form Jeremy Alcoba brought himself into contention with his customary late-race pace, although 2026 Champion Arenas was able to hold on. Arenas led the Tissot Superpole session, securing his third pole of the year, and his first since Aragon in May. He posted a 1’41.084s to beat Jorge Navarro to P1 on the Race 1 grid, with Oncu completing the front row. Arenas led for all but one lap throughout the 17-lap race, but that doesn’t tell the full story of the race. It took until Lap 12 for the Spanish rider to be more than half-a-second clear of Oncu, who was now falling into the clutches of Alcoba. On Lap 15, Alcoba got ahead of Oncu and trailed Arenas by 1.358s. A lap later and that gap had come down to 0.778s and it looked like the #52 could catch up to Arenas out in front. However, the race leader responded: on Lap 16, he set a 1’43.059s, and on Lap 17, he set a 1’42.742s to ensure Alcoba remained 0.533s down on him when they crossed the line. It meant Arenas claimed his fourth win of the season, and his first since Misano in June. Reflecting on his win and his battle with Oncu, Arenas said: “It was a great race for us. I felt super strong since the first laps this weekend. We managed the pace perfectly. I’m happy for my team and my people. It’s really special to win here at Jerez, with the crowd. Being able to stand on the podium in front of a home crowd is very nice. I was trying to keep my focus and ride well every lap. I was managing the rear tyre very well. I knew I had something else to try to put a bit more, but it wasn’t necessary. I just kept the same pace. I had to manage the front a little bit. I think we had a bit more in the second half of the race. I’m really proud of everyone and happy to be back on the top step.” Arenas was unable to make it a home double on Sunday. He was leading Race 2 when Tom Booth-Amos had two big moments under braking and clattered into the #75, sending him flying into the gravel. Arenas was taken to the medical centre for a check following the incident and he was diagnosed with multiple contusions. Booth-Amos was handed a Long Lap Penalty in the next race he competes in for irresponsible riding. Re-live Arenas’ title-winning campaign using the WorldSBK VideoPass !

signals.title: PEAKS AND TROUGHS: Strong weekends, late-race heartbreak and a difficult end to 2026
signals.summary: There were highs and lows at the 2026 season finale after a dramatic weekend of action at Jerez The MOTUL FIM Superbike World Championship headed to the Circuito de Jerez - Angel Nieto, Andalucia for the 2026 season finale. It was time for the Pirelli Spanish Round to round out a record-breaking season, but who ended the year on a high and who will be aiming to turn their fortunes around heading into next season? Sam Lowes (ELF Marc VDS Racing Team) headed to Jerez on the back of a tricky Estoril where he struggled to break into the top ten all weekend. The final round of the season was a different story, however, with the #14 only outside the top three once – in FP3. He split the two factory Ducatis in the Tissot Superpole session to claim second on the grid and converted that into P2 in Race 1 for his first rostrum since Cremona. Iker Lecuona (Aruba.it Racing - Ducati) got ahead of him in the Tissot Superpole Race but the Brit came home in third. In Race 2, it looked like Lowes would finish in fourth until some late-race rain meant he was able to hunt down Alvaro Bautista and snatch a podium on the final lap; jubilation for Lowes, heartbreak for the #19. Bautista’s future is still up in the air, with nothing confirmed about the two-time Champion. He has maintained that he wants to race, and his speed over Estoril and Jerez has proven he can still fight at the front. Ninth in Superpole became fourth in Race 1 and sixth in the Superpole Race, before a superb launch off the line in Race 2 meant he was in the podium places by Turn 1 on the opening lap. Running in third, he resisted earlier pressure from Lowes before building a gap of around 1.3 seconds by Lap 13. However, as rain started to fall, the British rider closed in and, while Bautista put up a valiant defence, Lowes got ahead at Turn 5 on the final lap to deny Bautista what could have been a final rostrum in WorldSBK. With 2026 done and nothing confirmed for the 63-time race winner, what will the future hold? Nicolo Bulega has re-written the history books this season. Prior to Jerez, the #11 had won more races in a row than anyone else, had claimed more podiums than anyone else and more wins in a single campaign than any other rider in WorldSBK history. So, perhaps it was no surprise he bowed out of WorldSBK with a few more records. He tied Ben Spies’ tally of poles from 2009 as the most recorded in a single season, with 11. He moved onto 50 victories in just 106 races, the quickest rider to achieve this; 44 races faster than previous record holder Troy Bayliss. With his hat-trick, he tied Bayliss’ tally of 52 wins for fifth place in the all-time list. The Superpole Race victory mean he moved onto 701 points, becoming the first rider to hit the 700-point mark. He finished on 726 out of a possible 744. After three years in WorldSBK, Bulega heads to MotoGP as he looks to mark his mark in Grand Prix racing. Watch as the #97's Yamaha R1 caught fire, ending the first race of the Spaniard's home round It’s been a tricky season for Yamaha in general this year, and it ended with just a handful of points to their name. Xavi Vierge was on course for points in Race 1 before his bike burst into flames down the start-finish straight, although both Andrea Locatelli (Pata Maxus Yamaha) and Remy Gardner (GYTR GRT Yamaha WorldSBK Team) did score. The undoubted high of the weekend would have been Vierge snatching P9 on the final lap in the Superpole Race as he took advantage of Tommy Bridewell (Superbike Advocates) and Alberto Surra (Motocorsa Racing) battling, before he finished the weekend in P12 in Race 2 as Yamaha’s only points scorer. The Japanese manufacturer will be hoping the 2027 rule changes and Jack Miller’s arrival, plus all the lessons learnt this season, can contribute to stronger performances next season. signals.title: Lecuona to replace Aldeguer at the Australian Grand Prix
signals.summary: 2026 WorldSBK runner-up Iker Lecuona will be back on MotoGP machinery this weekend as he steps in for the injured Fermin Aldeguer Iker Lecuona’s (Aruba.it Racing – Ducati) season is not quite over. After a double header in the MOTUL FIM Superbike World Championship, the #7 will now travel to Australia for this weekend’s Australian Grand Prix as he steps in for Fermin Aldeguer at Phillip Island. The BK8 Gresini Racing MotoGP rider was injured in a crash at Mandalika and needed surgery on a fracture to the base of his first metacarpal bone in his right hand. With the Spanish star still recovering, Lecuona will step aboard his Ducati machine. Lecuona has already raced for Gresini Ducati this season on a couple of occasions. The 2026 WorldSBK runner-up first replaced Alex Marquez at the Hungarian GP in June, where he claimed P7 in the Grand Prix. In August, he stepped in to replace Aldeguer at the British GP. He did not score points on that occasion. A social post from Gresini Racing said: “Fermin Aldeguer will not take part in the Australian GP. Iker Lecuona will once again be aboard the Ducati #54. Fermin is working to try to be fit to race in Malaysia in less than two weeks.” Re-live Lecuona’s best moments from 2026 using the WorldSBK VideoPass!

signals.title: Lecuona looks back on his breakout 2026: “This team changed my life…I’m in P2 because of how hard he pushed me”
signals.summary: The #7 was a constant force on the podium this season, and while he’s always aspired to more than P2, Lecuona is hanging his hat on the podium consistency in his first season with the team, aided by his departing teammate Spanish rider Iker Lecuona (Aruba.it Racing - Ducati) sealed his remarkable 2026 MOTUL FIM Superbike World Championship with a podium triple at his home Circuito de Jerez - Angel Nieto, Andalucia. The #7 can look back on what has been a historic 2026 season with pride, not only for the accomplishments of his team, but for the new heights to which he’s climbed, and rapidly acclimated. Lecuona landed a P3 finish to the season’s final Tissot Superpole event, just under half a second behind his 2026 Champion teammate Nicolo Bulega on pole, and around a tenth behind Sam Lowes (ELF Marc VDS Racing Team). He and the pair ahead of him ended Race 1’s first lap in the same order they set off in, and as the three heavyweights charged into the second half of the race, Lecuona ran two and a half seconds behind the #14. He pushed into the final laps, cutting the margin to P2 to 1.1s, but in the end, the #7 took P3 as he failed to close the gap. Sunday saw Lecuona jump out to his habitual P2 early in the Tissot Superpole Race as Sam Lowes fell farther back after a poor jump off the line at lights out. Despite setting sub-1’38s times on every lap except the opening and final laps, and from Lap 5 to the chequered flag setting faster lap times than Bulega in P1, Lecuona came up nearly eight tenths short of P1 behind the 2026 Champion. To round off the 2026 season, Lecuona charged ahead at lights out for the holeshot, and led for the first five turns of Race 2. At the heavy-braking ‘Dani Pedrosa’ corner, however, Bulega cut inside and shot ahead on the brakes to take P1. The gap was more than half a second by Lap 2, and more than a second by Lap 4. Lecuona came back to boxes after the chequered flag amid a torrential downpour at the circuit in P2 for the 27 th time this season, a tally that were it any other season, would be the talk of the entire WorldSBK paddock. The Spanish rider ends the year as runner-up in WorldSBK, 32 podium finishes in 36 races, and his first race win On his Sunday results and how he felt riding the last laps of the 2026 season, Lecuona said: “Saturday I struggled a lot, but Sunday morning, I found that changing some small details in my riding style helped me. I felt fast in the Superpole Race, and I recovered some time compared to Nicolo. In Race 2, however, he was much faster; he deserved it. At one point, the rain arrived, and the rear dropped a lot with the cold wind. I decided to finish the year in that position. I’m really happy. Like I said many times this year, this team changed my life. I was very happy riding that cooldown lap; I was smiling the entire time. I remembered all of this year. It’s been incredible.” To Lecuona, sharing a box with the #11 has brought its frustrations at times, as the #11 chafed behind Bulega’s hegemony over the top step of the podium. However, he also credits the #11 in part for the monumental step Lecuona has made in 2026: from two podiums over four seasons to the fourth-most podiums ever in a WorldSBK season. In his mind, that competition for P1 helped him get accustomed to finishing at the top of the order with regularity. That front-of-the-pack battle culminated in the #7 celebrating not just his Donington Park maiden win. But his maiden hat trick at Cremona for four wins in his first season in factory Ducati red. On the departure of his sparring partner to MotoGP, Lecuona said: “I felt sad when I first heard that his MotoGP rumours are true, because he pushed me so hard. When I was angry, or frustrated, or sad about finishing in P2. He told me that he’s been there too. I’m in P2 because of how hard he pushed me. I’m very happy for him, he had an amazing season. We always fight, aggressively, but always leaving a bit of space for each other. Honestly, I’m not happy that he’s leaving just so that I don’t have to compete with him. To me, if someone is better than me, I want to work and compete with them. Both of the other podiums I had before this year were because something happened up front; this year, I won four races. I feel more sad than happy to see him leave.” Look back on Lecuona’s breakthrough WorldSBK season OnDemand with the WorldSBK VideoPass!

signals.title: “It’s not easy to keep pushing until the end, we did that at Estoril, and now at Jerez” Bautista proud of his Jerez handiwork
signals.summary: While questions continue to circulate as to his seat for 2027, Bautista is staying present and proud of his and his team’s proud conclusion to the season The MOTUL FIM Superbike World Championship charged across the line and turned the page on its 2026 season, and while the Pirelli Spanish Round didn’t produce the rostrum return he had hoped, the final day at his beloved Circuito de Jerez - Angel Nieto, Andalucia showed the entire paddock that two-time WorldSBK Champion Alvaro Bautista still has the speed to fight for the podium. After an encouraging fourth-place finish to Saturday , it looked like all of the pieces were slowly clicking together for the #19 just in time for the season’s final pair of races on Sunday. Firing off at lights out from P9, Bautista got most of his work done early, stealing P8 from Independent Ducati Lorenzo Baldassarri (Team GoEleven) on the final Turn 13 of the opening lap. Lap 2 saw him take another position from Alberto Surra (Motocorsa Racing), cutting inside of the rookie rider at overtaking hotspot Turn 6 with slight contact to take seventh. Less than a minute later, while barreling down the straight into Lap 3, Bautista was brave on the brakes and passed Tommy Bridewell (Superbikes Advocates) for sixth place with eight laps still remaining. Try as he might, Bautista didn’t quite have the pace on Sunday morning to catch Alex Lowes (bimota by Kawasaki Racing Team) in P5 ahead of him. While he chopped it down to around six tenths by Lap 8, the margin hung at just under a second for most of the remainder of the contest, ushering Bautista to sixth place. The Spanish rider talks about his battle with Sam Lowes for the last step of the podium and talks about his future Sensing the lateness of the hour, Bautista propelled himself up to third by the end of Race 2’s opening lap, three positions forward from having started at the back of the second row. By Lap 3, the front pair were already distant on the horizon: #19 Iker Lecuona (Aruba.it Racing - Ducati) was nine tenths ahead, and Bulega over two seconds ahead. All went according to plan for the #19 as the race developed; he couldn’t quite shake Sam Lowes (ELF Marc VDS Racing Team) behind him, but his cushion had grown to just under two seconds by Lap 15; both figuratively and literally, however, the sky was getting darker for the #19 as dark clouds rolled in. The white flag was waved on Lap 16, and three minutes later, rain was reported in the first three sectors. By Lap 17, Bautista’s margin was down to nine tenths. By Lap 18, it was down to just 0.3s. With a return to the podium agonisingly close, just two laps away, he finished the penultimate Lap 19 with just two tenths in hand. With rain continuing to fall on track, the #14 completed his comeback for P3 on the final lap with a Turn 5 move, crossing the line in P3 after taking back half a second on Lap 16, and six tenths on Lap 18, thriving in the rainy conditions to steal away the podium from the #19. Bautista saw the Race 2 glass half-full, he said: “It wasn’t such a bad day. In the Superpole Race, it’s always difficult. Everyone is always pushing 100% from the start. I stayed close to the front positions, but not enough to catch them. Starting from the second row in Race 2, I had a better chance to stay at the front. I had a really good start, I overtook three riders into the first corner. It allowed me to sit third. I was riding well, felt good on the bike, and saw the gap behind me increasing. Behind me, Sam had me as a reference, and unfortunately, I lost some tyre pressure as I had stopped pushing as hard. After two or three laps, the tyres were difficult; I felt no grip, no contact, and I decided to at least finish the race. I’m happy, though, because when conditions were normal, I was strong and I improved my gap to other riders. The result isn’t what we deserved, but this is racing. You have to focus on the bike; you can’t think about the rain or about him catching you. I don’t feel frustrated; this time I had some problems, other times other riders have some problems. 2027 is still an unknown for the two-time World Champion, as Spanish rider Xavi Vierge will join the Barni Ducati box in his place, and he doesn’t have a seat confirmed for the season to come. The team waited for the rider back in their box, with his wife and two daughters waiting in the wings. Podium or not, Bautista showed his pedigree, and he will eagerly await news from his agent over the course of this offseason. Looking back on his season and looking ahead to 2027, Bautista said: “I’m so proud of the weekend we did. After a season like this, it’s not easy to recover. Results that didn’t come, the midseason injury, many circumstances that didn’t let us show our potential. It’s not easy to stay motivated and push until the end. We did that at Estoril, and we did that here, we have to be proud of this. It was fantastic to have my loved ones here. This weekend has been emotional overall, seeing the support from people who say, ‘Keep racing!’ In the box, it seemed like a goodbye, which it is from the team, but it’s been good to have them there waiting for me. I don’t know what’s next for me, I don’t have any new information. My manager is working on some proposals; I’ll call him this week. Let’s see if we have something motivating. I want to keep racing.” Watch back through Bautista’s best races in WorldSBK! Stream OnDemand now with the WorldSBK VideoPass!

signals.title: Fernandez-Manager über Trackhouse: «Haben ihnen ein Ultimatum gestellt!»
signals.summary: Erst spät in diesem Jahr einigten sich Raul Fernandez und Trackhouse darauf, auch 2027 und 2028 zusammenzuarbeiten. Weshalb es so lange dauerte und welches Angebot er noch auf seinem Tisch hatte. Nach seinem Vize-WM-Titel in der Moto2-Saison 2021 schaffte Raul Fernandez den Aufstieg in die MotoGP. Er dockte bei KTM Tech3 an – als Teamkollege des Australiers Remy Gardner. In seinem Rookie-Jahr 2022 tat sich Fernandez schwer mit der RC16, in der Gesamtwertung belegte er Rang 22. Zur Saison 2023 wechselte er ins RNF-Team, wo er an der Seite von Miguel Oliveira eine Aprilia RS-GP fuhr. Es sammelte damals insgesamt 51 WM-Punkte, was am Ende Gesamtrang 20 bedeutete. 2024 übernahm dann Trackhouse Racing das Ruder in dem Satellitenteam. Fernandez konnte sich weiter steigern, bis er 2025 beim Großen Preis von Australien seinen ersten MotoGP-Sieg holte. Letztes Jahr schaffte es der Spanier beim Saisonfinale in Valencia noch einmal auf das Podest. Ab der zweiten Saisonhälfte 2025 erzielte Raul Fernandez regelmäßig Top-Platzierungen. Im ersten Grand Prix 2026 bestätigte er seine Form, als er in Thailand zweimal auf das Podest raste. Es folgten zwei Sprintsiege (Mugello und Assen) und zwei GP-Podeste (Assen und Sachsenring). Der 25-Jährige zeigte starke Leistungen, doch etwas fehlte: Fernandez hatte für 2027 keinen Vertrag. Erst am 5. August, vor dem britischen Grand Prix, verkündete Trackhouse Racing die Vertragsverlängerung um zwei Jahre . Der Manager von Raul Fernandez ist der erfahrene Spanier Paco Sanchez. Er betreut auch Joan Mir. Im Gespräch mit SPEEDWEEK.com-Autor Manuel Pecino schilderte Sanchez, weshalb sich die Vertragsverhandlungen mit Trackhouse Racing so lange hinauszögerten und wo er noch überall angeklopft hatte. «Ich habe mit allen Herstellern gesprochen; nach und nach schlossen sich die Türen, und bei einigen stand der Deal kurz vor dem Abschluss, doch letztendlich entschieden sie sich für einen anderen Fahrer», erzählte Sanchez. «Erst beim Rennen in Assen kontaktierte mich KTM und unterbreitete uns ein Angebot für Tech3. Wir hatten ein Treffen mit dem Teambesitzer und erhielten ein verbindliches Angebot, dorthin zu wechseln. Erst da reagierte Trackhouse mit einem verbindlichen Angebot. Das Problem bei Trackhouse schien, als ob dort so etwas wie ein Machtvakuum herrschte.» Als Grund für dieses Vakuum nannte Sanchez die Ankündigung, dass Teamchef Davide Brivio die Struktur Ende 2026 verlassen wird. «Es war unklar, wer für die Vertragsverlängerungen der Fahrer zuständig war. Justin Marks war in diesem Jahr bis zu jenem Zeitpunkt nur bei zwei Rennen dabei, das dritte war jenes in Silverstone. Und offensichtlich verfügt er nicht über die Erfahrung in der MotoGP», meinte Sanchez. «Er musste ein Team umstrukturieren, das nach der Bekanntgabe des Abgangs von Davide etwas ins Wanken geraten war. Dann musste er sich auf die Suche nach einem Teammanager machen, was die Verlängerung der Verträge bzw. die Verpflichtung neuer Fahrer etwas verzögerte, und genau das hat ihre Entscheidung hinausgezögert. Aber als wir die Möglichkeit hatten, zu KTM zu wechseln, haben wir ihnen ein Ultimatum gestellt, und ihre Reaktion erfolgte umgehend: Sie legten einen Vertrag auf den Tisch, und Rauls Absicht war es immer, bei ihnen zu bleiben.» Geregelt wurden unterdessen auch die weiteren wichtigen Rollen. Mit Enea Bastianini kommt ein MotoGP-Großkalilber als Teamkollege. In der Box gesteuert wird das Team dann vom ebenfalls sehr erfahrenen Francesco Guidotti. signals.title: Weltpremiere in Austin: Die MotoGP ist beim US-GP der Formel 1 zu Gast
signals.summary: Beim Formel-1-Wochenende in Austin werden Ende Oktober Nicolo Bulega, Dani Pedrosa, Andrea Dovizioso und Lorenzo Savadori den US-amerikanischen Fans die MotoGP-WM näherbringen. Vom 23. bis 25. Oktober gastiert die MotoGP-WM in Australien. Am gleichen Wochenende findet auf der anderen Seite der Welt der US-GP der Formel 1 statt. In Austin (Texas) wird dennoch die Königsklasse der Motorrad-WM im Rahmen eines Show-Events am Samstag präsent sein. So werden Superbike-Weltmeister Nicolo Bulega (Ducati) sowie die Testfahrer Dani Pedrosa (KTM), Andrea Dovizioso (Yamaha) und Lorenzo Savadori (Trackhouse Aprilia) den Formel-1-Fans auf dem Circuit of the Americas (COTA) im Rahmen einer Demonstrationsfahrt die seltene Gelegenheit bieten, die MotoGP-Raketen live zu erleben. Mit dem Show-Event und weiteren Fan-Aktivitäten ist die MotoGP erstmals in ein Formel-1-Grand-Prix-Wochenende eingebunden. Erwartet werden beim US-GP mehr als 400.000 Fans. Die MotoGP-Teams und -Fahrer werden von Donnerstag bis Sonntag vor Ort in Austin sein. «Es ist immer etwas Besonderes, auf dem COTA, einer der legendärsten Rennstrecken der Welt, ein MotoGP-Motorrad zu fahren», freut sich Dani Pedrosa. «Der Grand Prix der Vereinigten Staaten ist ein wahrhaft einzigartiges und besonderes Ereignis im F1-Kalender, das unglaublich viele Zuschauer anzieht und eine großartige Gelegenheit bietet, den Fans einen Vorgeschmack darauf zu geben, was die MotoGP so spannend macht. Die Geschwindigkeit, der Sound und die Leistung dieser Motorräder muss man live erleben, und ich freue mich darauf, das mit allen in Austin zu teilen.» Nicolo Bulega, nächstjähriger MotoGP-Rookie bei VR46 Ducati, ergänzte: «Das ist eine fantastische Gelegenheit, die MotoGP vor einem der größten Publikumsmengen im weltweiten Motorsport zu präsentieren. Die Atmosphäre auf dem COTA ist immer unglaublich, und es wird ein besonderes Erlebnis sein, vor so vielen Fans ein MotoGP-Motorrad zu fahren. MotoGP-Motorräder sind mit nichts anderem zu vergleichen, und hoffentlich werden die Runden zeigen, wie spektakulär unser Sport ist. Wir freuen uns darauf, eine großartige Show zu bieten und den Fans einen Vorgeschmack darauf zu geben, was sie erwarten können, wenn ich 2027 mit der MotoGP nach Austin zurückkehre.» Der US-GP der MotoGP-WM findet nächstes Jahr vom 23. bis 25. April statt. Dieses Show-Event stellt einen weiteren Schritt dar, um die MotoGP einem größeren Publikum näher zu bringen und neue Fans zu gewinnen – ganz im Sinne von Liberty Media. signals.title: LCR Honda: David Alonso wurde als Teamkollege von Johann Zarco bestätigt
signals.summary: Nachdem das Honda-Werksteam die Verpflichtung von Diogo Moreira als Teamkollege von Fabio Quartararo ab der MotoGP-Saison 2027 bekannt gegeben hatte, wurde David Alonso beim LCR-Team bestätigt. Es zeichnete sich jedoch ab, dass Diogo Moreira von LCR ins Werksteam befördert wird und Alonso 2027 dessen Platz in der Truppe von Lucio Cecchinello einnehmen wird. Am 20. Oktober ging es dann Schlag auf Schlag: Zuerst verabschiedete sich LCR Honda von Moreira, wenige Minuten danach wurde der Brasilianer beim Honda-Werksteam offiziell bestätigt – und David Alonso wiederum bei LCR. «Ich bin unglaublich aufgeregt und kann es kaum erwarten, mit einem Team wie LCR Honda den Sprung in die MotoGP zu schaffen», freute sich David Alonsio. «Es ist ein hochprofessionelles Team mit einem reichen Erfahrungsschatz, und ich glaube, dass es der perfekte Ort ist, um meinen Anpassungs- und Lernprozess in der MotoGP zu beginnen. Es ist ein wichtiger Schritt, und ich kann es kaum erwarten, dieses neue Abenteuer zu beginnen. Ein Traum wird wahr, und das ist erst der Anfang.» Als eines der vielversprechendsten Talente im Motorradrennsport hat Alonso in den letzten vier Saisons 32 Podestplätze erzielt, darunter 20 Siege. 2024 holte er sich den Moto3-Weltmeistertitel. 2026, in seiner zweiten Moto2-Saison, liegt er vor den letzten fünf Saisonrennen mit 166 Punkten auf Gesamtrang 5. 2027 wird er den nächsten Schritt in seiner Karriere machen und in die Königsklasse aufsteigen. signals.title: Schock für Yamaha: Toprak Razgatlioglu fällt für die restliche Saison aus
signals.summary: Bei seinem Crash in Indonesien verletzte sich Toprak Razgatlioglu an seiner rechten Schulter. Nun bestätigte Pramac Yamaha, dass er operiert werden muss und die restliche MotoGP-Saison 2026 ausfällt. Bei einem heftigen Crash im zweiten freien Training in Indonesien hatte sich Toprak Razgatlioglu die rechte Schulter ausgekugelt. Das Sprintrennen am Samstag fuhr der 30-Jährige unter Schmerzen zu Ende, doch im Grand Prix am Sonntag musste er nach acht Runden das Handtuch werfen, weil ihm die Kraft fehlte. Nach weiteren medizinischen Untersuchungen in Mailand steht nun fest, dass sich der Yamaha-Pilot am 26. Oktober einer Operation unterziehen muss. Dies bestätigte Pramac am heutigen Dienstag. Besonders bitter: Toprak wird nicht nur den Großen Preis von Australien verpassen, er wird für die restliche MotoGP-Saison 2026 ausfallen. Yamaha-Testfahrer Augusto Fernandez wird ihn bei den kommenden Rennen ersetzen. Toprak bedauert vor allem, dass er beim Australien-GP nicht antreten kann. Dieser findet in diesem Jahr das letzte Mal auf Phillip Island statt. «Ich bin äußerst enttäuscht, den Grand Prix von Australien verpassen zu müssen. Phillip Island ist eine meiner Lieblingsrennstrecken und ein Ort, an dem ich während meiner Superbike-Karriere einige ganz besondere Momente erlebt habe. Ich hatte mich sehr auf die Gelegenheit gefreut, dort auf dem MotoGP-Motorrad anzutreten, was diese Situation noch schwerer zu akzeptieren macht», ist der Superbike-Weltmeister von 2025 enttäuscht. «Nach weiteren medizinischen Untersuchungen im Anschluss an den Sturz in Mandalika stellte sich heraus, dass meine Schulterverletzung schwerwiegender ist, als wir zunächst angenommen hatten. Daher werde ich mich in den kommenden Tagen einer Operation unterziehen, um mir die besten Chancen auf eine vollständige Genesung und eine Rückkehr zu 100 Prozent zu sichern. Das war keine leichte Entscheidung, aber nach Rücksprache mit den Ärzten und den Menschen, die mir am nächsten stehen, sind wir überzeugt, dass dies der richtige Schritt für meine Zukunft ist.» Pramac Yamaha versicherte, Toprak bei der Rehabilitation voll zu unterstützen. «Es tut uns sehr leid für Toprak, da wir wissen, wie sehr er sich darauf gefreut hat, in Phillip Island zu fahren und seine Reise mit der YZR-M1 fortzusetzen», meinte Teamdirektor Gino Borsoi. «Er hat hart daran gearbeitet, sich an die MotoGP anzupassen, und es ist enttäuschend, dass diese Verletzung ihn daran hindern wird, diesen Prozess in den kommenden Rennen fortzusetzen. Seine Gesundheit hat jedoch Vorrang, und wir werden ihn während seiner Genesung unterstützen und freuen uns darauf, ihn wieder auf dem Motorrad zu sehen, sobald er bereit ist. Gleichzeitig heißen wir Augusto Fernandez willkommen, der in Phillip Island für Toprak einspringen wird, bis dieser wieder einsatzbereit ist. Als Testfahrer von Yamaha kennt er das Motorrad gut, und wir freuen uns, ihn für diese Rennen im Team zu haben. Wir werden gemeinsam daran arbeiten, das Beste aus dieser Gelegenheit zu machen, und wünschen Toprak eine erfolgreiche Operation und eine reibungslose Genesung.» Topraks Teamkollege Jack Miller wird in Australien seinen letzten Heim-GP in der MotoGP-Klasse bestreiten. «Ich möchte Jack alles Gute für seinen Heim-Grand-Prix wünschen. Vor heimischem Publikum zu fahren, ist immer etwas Besonderes, und da dies das letzte MotoGP-Rennen auf Phillip Island ist, hoffe ich, dass er ein fantastisches Wochenende genießen und ein großartiges Ergebnis erzielen kann. Ich werde ihn und das gesamte Team aus der Ferne anfeuern», sagte Toprak. Für Toprak Razgatlioglu ist die MotoGP-Rookie-Saison nun vorzeitig zu Ende gegangen. Er tat sich das ganze Jahr schwer mit der Umstellung auf das MotoGP-Bike und mit der schwächelnden M1. An 17 Rennwochenenden konnte er 18 WM-Punkte sammeln. 2027 wird er gemeinsam mit Yamaha in die neue MotoGP-Ära – mit dem 850-ccm-Bike und den Pirelli-Reifen – starten. signals.summary: Am 20. Oktober bestätigte HRC, dass Diogo Moreira 2027 ins Honda-Werksteam wechseln wird. Oktober kam die offizielle Bestätigung dafür. Der 22-jährige Brasilianer wird nächstes Jahr – wenn die neuen MotoGP-Regeln in Kraft treten – an der Seite von Fabio Quartararo fahren. Honda kann somit 2027 auf ein Fahrerduo vertrauen, dass langjährige Erfahrung in der Königsklasse mit jugendlichem Potenzial vereint. «Es ist ein fantastisches Gefühl, zum Honda-MotoGP-Werksteam zu stoßen – davon träumt jeder Fahrer, wenn er noch jung ist», freute sich Moreira. «Ich möchte mich bei allen bei HRC bedanken, die mir ihr Vertrauen geschenkt haben und den nächsten Schritt in diesem Projekt möglich gemacht haben. Bislang haben wir im Jahr 2026 großartige Arbeit geleistet, um uns an das Motorrad anzupassen, und die Aussichten für die Zukunft sind nach dem, was wir bisher gesehen haben, bereits sehr positiv.» Moreira nahm auch die Gelegenheit wahr, um sich beim LCR-Team zu bedanken: «Natürlich muss ich mich auch bei allen bei LCR bedanken, die mir bei meiner Eingewöhnung in die MotoGP geholfen haben – das gesamte Team war für diese Entwicklung von entscheidender Bedeutung. Ich freue mich auf das nächste Jahr und darauf, Honda dabei zu helfen, wieder dorthin zurückzukehren, wo sie hingehören.» LCR-Pilot Diogo Moreira zeigt in seiner MotoGP-Rookie-Saison beachtliche Leistungen. Er erzielte bislang mehrere Top-10-Platzierungen, zuletzt stürmte er im Sprint in Japan auf das Podest. Sein Wechsel ins Werksteam hat sich schon seit längerer Zeit abgezeichnet. «Moreira hat sich schon immer schnell an neue Motorräder anpassen können, vom Motocross über die Moto3 und Moto2 bis hin zur MotoGP. Das ist das Zeichen eines talentierten Fahrers, und wir als HRC wollen Diogo auch beim nächsten Schritt seiner Karriere und bei unserem Vorhaben, wieder um die Weltmeisterschaft mitzukämpfen, weiterhin unterstützen», betonte Yuzuru Ishikawa, General Manager Motorcycle Racing Division bei der Honda Racing Corporation. «Wir verfügen in der kommenden Saison über eine äußerst konkurrenzfähige Fahreraufstellung bei Honda HRC Castrol und dem LCR-Team, und ich bin mir sicher, dass sich all diese Fahrer gegenseitig antreiben werden, nicht nur, um ihr Niveau auf der Strecke zu steigern, sondern auch, um den Ingenieuren von HRC dabei zu helfen, das bestmögliche Motorrad in dieser neuen Ära des Rennsports zu entwickeln.» Nach Durststrecke: KTM ist zurück am Podium! signals.title: Joan Mir zog Karriereende in Betracht – dann kam Gresini Ducati auf ihn zu
signals.summary: Der ehemalige MotoGP-Weltmeister Joan Mir wollte auch 2027 für ein Werksteam fahren – doch das klappte nicht. Sein Manager Paco Sanchez erzählt, weshalb das Angebot von Gresini unwiderstehlich war. 2017 dominerte Joan Mir die Moto3-WM. Er holte zehn Siege und gewann überlegen den Titel. Danach folgte der Aufstieg in die Moto2-Klasse, wo er bereits nach einer Saison in die MotoGP aufstieg. In der Königsklasse schaffte er es 2020, in seinem zweiten Jahr, mit der Suzuki GSX-RR den WM-Titel zu holen. Die Saison 2021 beendete er als WM-Dritter. Nach dem MotoGP-Ausstieg von Suzuki wechselte Joan Mir 2023 ins Honda-Werksteam. Seitdem hat der Spanier mit der schwächelnden RC213V zu kämpfen. In den letzten drei Jahren belegte er die WM-Ränge 22, 21 und 15. Letztes Jahr schaffte es Mir immerhin zweimal auf das Podest. 2026 holte er bislang nur 33 WM-Punkte, derzeit liegt er in der Gesamtwertung auf Rang 18. Zum Vergleich: Teamkollege Luca Marini hat 108 Punkte auf seinem Konto und ist 12. Joan Mir ist schnell, das steht außer Frage. Doch beim Versuch, alles aus der Honda herauszuholen, überfährt er das Motorrad oft – die Folge daraus sind sehr viele Stürze. Schon früh in dieser Saison war klar, dass es für ihn 2027 kein Platz mehr bei HRC geben wird. Honda wird nächstes Jahr im Werksteam mit einem neuen Fahreraufgebot in die 850er-Ära starten – mit Fabio Quartararo und Diogo Moreira. Für Joan Mir gab es für 2027 zunächst wenig Optionen – bis Gresini Racing auf ihn zukam. «Meine Priorität war es, ein Werksteam für Joan zu finden. Wir sahen dann aber, dass das nicht klappte. Joan dachte über das Aufhören nach – falls wir kein Werksteam finden würden. Er zog nicht einmal die Superbike-WM oder etwas anderes in Betracht. Seine Situation war klar: 'Wenn ich kein wettbewerbsfähiges Motorrad habe, höre ich auf, und ich gehe nach Hause'», erzählte sein Manager Paco Sanchez im Interview von SPEEDWEEK.com-Autor Manuel Pecino. «Dann war es Gresini, die mich anriefen. Ich habe ein sehr gutes Verhältnis zu ihnen. Also rief mich Michele (Masini) an und sagte: ‘Paco, wir sind daran interessiert, über Joan zu sprechen.’ Daraufhin sagte ich ihm: ‘Ich werde zu euch kommen, um zu reden, aber ich bin mir nicht sicher, ob Joan in einem Satellitenteam weitermachen will.’ Ich habe mich dann mit Joan getroffen; sowohl im Namen von Gresini als auch von Ducati war Gigi Dall’Igna bei dem Treffen dabei. Er sagte ihm, dass er ein reines Werksmotorrad bekommen würde, dass er offizielle Werksunterstützung erhalten würde und dass er, wenn er die von ihm erwarteten Ergebnisse erzielen würde, dasselbe Motorrad (wie die Werksfahrer, Anm.) haben würde. Natürlich kommen die Upgrades manchmal etwas später, aber er würde dasselbe Motorrad haben wie Marc und Pedro.» Für Joan Mir klang das Angebot sehr interessant – er nahm es an. «Joan hat von da an die finanzielle Seite vergessen, das trat für ihn in den Hintergrund», so Sanchez. «Er legte den Schwerpunkt auf die Chance, wieder ein wettbewerbsfähiges Motorrad zu haben. Er will sich wieder als Fahrer fühlen, der um die Weltmeisterschaft kämpft – der Rennen gewinnt und ganz vorne mitfährt.» 2027 wird Joan Mir eine Ducati Desmosedici mit 850 ccm fahren. Es ist davon auszugehen, dass dieses Bike in er neuen MotoGP-Ära sehr konkurrenzfähig sein wird – so wie die Ducati mit 1000 ccm. Nach Durststrecke: KTM ist zurück am Podium! signals.title: Phillip Island: Der Zeitplan für den Großen Preis von Australien 2026
signals.summary: Vom 23. bis 25. Oktober gastiert die MotoGP-WM auf Phillip Island. Wer den Australien-GP live mitverfolgen möchte, muss früh aufstehen. Und: Am Sonntag erfolgt die Umstellung auf die Winterzeit. Mit Ausnahme von 2020 und 2021 (Absage aufgrund der Corona-Pandemie) findet auf dem Phillip Island Circuit seit 1997 das einzige Rennen der Motorrad-WM auf dem australischen Kontinent statt. Die Piste überzeugt nicht nur mit ihrer eindrucksvollen Landschaft direkt am Meer, sondern bringt den Fans als eine der schnellsten Strecken im MotoGP-Kalender jedes Jahr spannende Rennen. Der Rundkurs misst mit seinen fünf Rechts- und sieben Linkskurven 4,45 km und hat eine 900 m lange Start-Ziel-Gerade.
